title: Dunder Mifflin Infinity

jokes.text: Toby's memo about PDA — Michael immediately assumes it's about him and Jan, then reveals embarrassing details about their office encounter
jokes.setup: Toby sends a generic PDA memo to the office. Michael reads it and challenges Toby.
jokes.punchline: Michael launches into an unprompted confession that it was consensual, that they were discreet, and that most people had left — revealing far more than anyone suspected or wanted to know.
jokes.explanation: Textbook Michael Scott oversharing. The structure is excellent — the memo is innocent, but Michael's defensive guilt-spiral reveals progressively more damning information ('I will have you know that was consensual... most people had left by that point'). Deep character integration: only Michael would publicly incriminate himself while trying to defend himself. The escalating specificity is what makes it land.

jokes.text: Is this about me and Jan in my office? Because I will have you know that that was consensual. What we did has nothing to do with you or anyone here. I don't think anyone heard anything. We were very discreet and most people had left by that point.
jokes.setup: Toby mentions the PDA memo is about someone in the office. Michael assumes it's about him and Jan.
jokes.punchline: Michael over-explains their privacy and discretion in a way that reveals far more than he intends — including that people could have heard, that not everyone had left, and that it was apparently notable enough to require a memo.
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael oversharing — each qualifier he adds digs the hole deeper. 'Most people had left by that point' is the best line, accidentally confirming an audience existed. Well-structured escalation within a single speech.

jokes.text: What I think you should do is roll up the memo real tight...
jokes.setup: Michael is indignant about the PDA memo and begins to tell Toby what to do with it.
jokes.punchline: The implication — interrupted before he can finish — is obviously that Toby should shove it somewhere. The cutoff makes the joke cleaner than if he'd completed it.
jokes.explanation: Familiar joke construction but the interruption saves it from being too crude. The restraint is funnier than completion would be. Competent but not inventive.

jokes.text: For the record, I have never been involved with anyone at work in any capacity.
jokes.setup: Toby clarifies the memo wasn't about Michael, and adds this statement about himself.
jokes.punchline: Toby's quiet, sad insistence that he has never been involved with anyone — which reads as a tragic confession of his romantic life rather than a defense — is delivered deadpan, making it funnier.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Toby — he means it as professional clarification, but it lands as a window into his miserable existence. The comedy is in what he doesn't say. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: All right, the complaint was about Jim and Pam.
jokes.setup: Michael assumes the PDA memo is about him and Jan. Toby has been deflecting.
jokes.punchline: Toby finally reveals it's Jim and Pam — a complete reversal that recontextualizes the entire preceding scene.
jokes.explanation: The misdirection pays off cleanly — we've been watching Michael embarrass himself defending something he wasn't even accused of. The reveal reframes everything and functions as a satisfying structural punchline for the cold open.

jokes.text: Tuna! Awesome! I knew it. To the two of you.
jokes.setup: The office learns Jim and Pam are dating. Various coworkers react.
jokes.punchline: Andy's 'Tuna! Awesome!' is both enthusiastic and reveals his only emotional connection to Jim is the nickname he invented. Kevin and Phyllis treat it like a wedding toast.
jokes.explanation: Andy calling Jim 'Tuna' in a moment of genuine emotion is a good character beat — his enthusiasm is disproportionate to their actual relationship, which is the joke.

jokes.text: Everyone, this is a day that will live in infamy, because today is the day that Jim and Pam become one.
jokes.setup: The office discovers Jim and Pam are dating. Michael seizes the moment for a speech.
jokes.punchline: Michael invokes 'a day that will live in infamy' — a phrase associated with Pearl Harbor — to describe two coworkers dating. The grandiosity is wildly disproportionate.
jokes.explanation: Michael's tendency to invoke historical gravitas for mundane events is well-worn by this point in the series, but 'day that will live in infamy' is a strong specific choice. The follow-up 'become one' tips into wedding ceremony territory, compounding the absurdity.

jokes.text: Actually, we've been dating for a couple of months.
jokes.setup: Michael is giving a grandiose speech about the day Jim and Pam 'become one.'
jokes.punchline: Jim's flat, matter-of-fact correction deflates the entire ceremony Michael has constructed.
jokes.explanation: Jim's role as the straight man deflating Michael's excess is perfectly executed. The economy is near-perfect — one sentence, maximum comic contrast. This is Jim at his best.

jokes.text: My heart soars with the eagle's nest.
jokes.setup: Michael is emotionally overwhelmed by Jim and Pam's relationship news.
jokes.punchline: Michael attempts a poetic expression but produces something that is grammatically and idiomatically nonsensical — eagles don't 'soar with nests,' and the phrase means nothing.
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional Michael Scott writing. 'My heart soars with the eagle's nest' sounds profound until you parse it — it's complete gibberish delivered with total sincerity. It's not random nonsense; it's the specific kind of half-formed poetic impulse Michael would have, reaching for Hallmark-card sentiment and landing in absurdism. Quotable, specific to the character, and earns its score.

jokes.text: I don't see it. I think they both could do better. It's not a surprise to me. Pam is the office mattress.
jokes.setup: The office is celebrating Jim and Pam's relationship. Cut to Angela's reaction.
jokes.punchline: Angela's cutting assessment — particularly 'Pam is the office mattress' — is shockingly mean and completely in character for someone who has been secretly dating Dwight.
jokes.explanation: The irony — Angela calling Pam promiscuous while she herself is secretly dating a coworker — is rich but unspoken, adding a rewatch layer. 'Office mattress' from the primly judgmental Angela is a great line. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Jim Halpert's off the market. Guess who just became the best-looking single guy in the office?
jokes.setup: The office learns Jim and Pam are together. Andy reacts in a talking head.
jokes.punchline: Andy congratulates himself on being promoted to 'best-looking single guy' by Jim's departure from the dating pool — a self-assessment both delusional and endearing.
jokes.explanation: Classic Andy — the smug self-congratulation on an achievement he didn't earn, phrased like a sports announcement. The setup-punchline within the talking head is clean and the character voice is spot-on.

jokes.text: That's what she said. / 'Can you make that straighter?' / 'That job looks hard.' / 'You should put your mouth on that.' — How can you even use that one naturally? — Blowing up balloons, I thought.
jokes.setup: Jim asks about a decoration being hung, Michael says 'that's what she said.' Jim challenges him on how he uses it naturally.
jokes.punchline: Michael rattles off three more setups he has stockpiled for balloons, revealing he actively pre-plans 'that's what she said' situations. 'Blowing up balloons, I thought' is the kicker.
jokes.explanation: This transcends the running gag by adding a meta-layer: Michael doesn't just reflexively say it, he actively strategizes around it, pre-loading setups for balloon-inflation scenarios. Jim's question 'how can you even use that one naturally?' is the key — it forces Michael to reveal his methodology, which is the real joke. Genuinely clever use of a familiar bit.

jokes.text: It's a feral barn cat. I trapped him last night and I'm giving him to you as a replacement cat for the one I destroyed. Her name was Sprinkles. And his name is Garbage. Mose calls him Garbage 'cause he likes to eat garbage.
jokes.setup: Dwight approaches Angela with a gift after previously killing her cat Sprinkles.
jokes.punchline: The gift is a feral barn cat named 'Garbage' — the name itself is the punchline, and Dwight's earnest explanation that Mose named him because he eats garbage makes it worse/better.
jokes.explanation: Everything about this is perfectly Dwight: the transactional approach to grief, the immediate pivot to practicality ('he's a useful cat'), the name 'Garbage' presented without irony, and the casual mention of Mose as if that explains everything. 'He killed an entire family of raccoons' as a selling point is inspired. This is one of the episode's best jokes because every word is character-specific and it builds beautifully.

jokes.text: He killed an entire family of raccoons. Look at him.
jokes.setup: Dwight is trying to convince Angela to accept Garbage as a replacement for Sprinkles.
jokes.punchline: Dwight presents raccoon massacre as a credential, delivered with genuine pride and the implicit belief that Angela will find this persuasive.
jokes.explanation: The escalation within the sales pitch is excellent — Dwight moves from 'he eats garbage' to 'he's a useful cat' to 'he killed an entire raccoon family.' Each fact is worse, each delivered as if it's obviously a selling point. The 'Look at him' tag is perfect deadpan.

jokes.text: Oh, well, you know those are only for, you know, 'relationships.' So if this is just a casual thing, there's no need.
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam ask Toby if they need to sign relationship disclosure forms. Toby has an obvious crush on Pam.
jokes.punchline: Toby suggests their relationship might be 'casual' and therefore not require paperwork — a technically professional response that reads as desperate wishful thinking from a man with obvious feelings for Pam.
jokes.explanation: The cringe comes from understanding what Toby is actually doing — using his HR authority to implant doubt. 'If this is just a casual thing' is Toby grasping at straws. The comedy is completely in the subtext.

jokes.text: Let's just wait and see what happens.
jokes.setup: Pam clarifies their relationship is 'pretty official.' Toby is asked directly if they need to sign forms.
jokes.punchline: Toby's response — 'let's just wait and see what happens' — is HR-speak that makes no sense in context and reveals he's stalling, presumably hoping their relationship fails.
jokes.explanation: Toby's 'let's wait and see' is simultaneously unprofessional and pathetic — it's an HR rep advising against HR compliance because of his own feelings. Jim and Pam's confused beat reaction makes it land.

jokes.text: He has facial hair. Look at him. All grown up and no place to go.
jokes.setup: Ryan returns to the Scranton branch as the new VP. Michael greets him.
jokes.punchline: Michael's 'all grown up and no place to go' is condescending to someone who is now his boss — he's treating the VP as a wayward child, completely unaware of the power dynamic.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Michael's total unawareness that his condescension toward Ryan is now career-threatening. Decent but not especially crafted.

jokes.text: Hello, Mr. Sonny Crockett. I'm Tubbs.
jokes.setup: Ryan has returned with a beard. Michael continues to greet him with TV character references.
jokes.punchline: Michael compares Ryan's beard to Miami Vice's Sonny Crockett and then introduces himself as Tubbs — the Black detective in the show — without any apparent awareness of the racial dimension.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of the Miami Vice reference (a show from before Ryan's time) and Michael's self-identification as Tubbs without reflection is classic Michael blundering through cultural touchstones. The joke has layers the character doesn't intend.

jokes.text: You're gonna have to treat me the same way you treated Jan. / That's a little kinky. I don't swing that way. / I think Ryan has a gay crush on me.
jokes.setup: Ryan asks the office to treat him professionally as their new boss, specifically like they treated Jan.
jokes.punchline: Michael immediately sexualizes the comparison to Jan (his girlfriend), then reads Ryan's exasperation as a 'gay crush.' Michael's subsequent talking head confirms he genuinely believes this.
jokes.explanation: The talking head punchline ('Ryan has a gay crush on me') is a solid payoff to Michael misreading a professional correction as flirtation. Competent Michael Scott material without reaching the top tier.

jokes.text: Ryan snapped at me. But there was this twinkle in his eye that I picked up on, which said, 'Dude, we're friends. I'm doing this for appearances.' ... 'And I miss you, man, and I love you.' His words.
jokes.setup: Ryan has just publicly told Michael to stop and behave professionally. Michael does a talking head about it.
jokes.punchline: Michael invents an elaborate internal monologue for Ryan — including 'I miss you, man, and I love you' — then tags it 'His words,' claiming Ryan actually said this.
jokes.explanation: The escalating fantasy Michael constructs for Ryan — each line more tender and delusional than the last — culminates in 'His words.' which is a superb tag. It recontextualizes everything: Michael isn't summarizing his impression, he's insisting Ryan literally said this. The construction is excellent, and 'his words' alone is quotable. One of the episode's best jokes.

jokes.text: What if we don't want to use a BlackBerry because they are stupid and pointless?
jokes.setup: Ryan announces all essential personnel will receive company BlackBerries.
jokes.punchline: Dwight asks this as a serious question, framing his Luddite objection as legitimate corporate feedback.
jokes.explanation: Solid Dwight moment — his contempt for technology is in character and the deadpan framing as a legitimate question is good. Not standout but functional.

jokes.text: You should call it Dunder Mifflinfinity. You know, push the words together.
jokes.setup: Ryan presents the Dunder Mifflin Infinity initiative. Andy raises his hand for a question.
jokes.punchline: Andy's contribution is to suggest a branding change — smashing the words together — delivered with complete sincerity as if this is a valuable insight.
jokes.explanation: Andy's networking-class enthusiasm applied to a useless idea. The 'you know, push the words together' explanation as if he needs to clarify is what elevates it from a throwaway. Good Andy.

jokes.text: Kelly Kapoor? Can we speak privately about our relationship?
jokes.setup: Ryan opens the floor for questions after his presentation.
jokes.punchline: Kelly raises her hand and asks to speak privately about their (romantic) relationship in the middle of a company-wide business meeting.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Kelly — completely unable to separate professional and personal contexts. The formality of raising her hand to ask a completely inappropriate question makes it funnier. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: ...Sammy, Phyllis, the chick you hit with the car, we're goners.
jokes.setup: Stanley is listing which employees he thinks are in danger of being pushed out for being older.
jokes.punchline: Stanley refers to Meredith — whom Michael literally hit with his car — as 'the chick you hit with the car,' a casual callout that treats a traumatic incident as just a descriptor.
jokes.explanation: The callback is casually inserted mid-list, which is the joke — Stanley treats 'the chick you hit with the car' as her established identifier, not as an event that requires explanation. The nonchalance is what makes it land. Good economy and dark comedy.

jokes.text: Dwight and Angela — dating. Have been for six months. / No, they have been dating for, like, two years. Since before your barbecue.
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam are newly public as a couple. Jim reveals what he thinks is a bombshell secret — Dwight and Angela are dating. Pam reveals she already knew.
jokes.punchline: Pam not only knew, but corrects Jim's timeline — they've been together far longer than Jim thought, and Pam has been sitting on this information.
jokes.explanation: The comic escalation — Jim thinks six months is the bombshell, Pam says two years — works well. The mutual 'we should have started dating earlier' conclusion is a nice button. The rewatch bonus comes from knowing the full Dwight-Angela arc.

jokes.text: We should have started dating, like, a long time ago.
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam realize they've both been sitting on mutual secrets and information about their coworkers.
jokes.punchline: Pam's conclusion — they should've dated sooner — frames their romantic success in terms of intelligence-sharing efficiency.
jokes.explanation: A sweet-funny button line. The comedy is understated — dating framed as an information-sharing partnership. Light but effective.

jokes.text: Oh, I didn't know you guys were in here. I couldn't see your hands.
jokes.setup: Toby walks into the break room and finds Jim and Pam together. They clarify they're just sitting there.
jokes.punchline: Toby's 'I couldn't see your hands' implies he suspected (or perhaps hoped to catch) physical activity — a deeply awkward thing for HR to say to employees just sitting at a table.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. 'I couldn't see your hands' is extraordinarily weird — it implies Toby was checking, which is creepy, and it frames Toby's Pam obsession in a new, unsettling way. Economical and character-perfect. The audience discomfort is part of the comedy.

jokes.text: Hey, Pam, by the way, it's great that you're dating. But when a new client calls, you just have to randomly assign them to a salesperson. You can't base who gets new clients on who you're sleeping with that week.
jokes.setup: Toby follows up his hand-comment with a professional note to Pam about client assignment.
jokes.punchline: 'Who you're sleeping with that week' — framing a two-month committed relationship as a revolving weekly arrangement — is either an attempt to undermine the relationship or a spectacularly clumsy HR phrasing.
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'that week' is doing enormous comedy work — it subtly frames Pam as promiscuous (Angela-style) while Toby probably means it clinically. Jim and Pam's reaction beat makes it land. The episode's button on the Toby-cringe section is 'And that is why we waited so long to tell people' which is the clean payoff.

jokes.text: And that is why we waited so long to tell people.
jokes.setup: Toby has just said Jim and Pam shouldn't base client assignments on 'who you're sleeping with that week.' Jim and Pam exchange a look.
jokes.punchline: Jim's talking-head explanation — that Toby's behavior is why they kept the relationship secret — is the payoff to the entire PDA/Toby opening arc.
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural payoff. Everything that Toby has done in this episode — the passive-aggressive memo, the 'casual thing' deflection, the 'I couldn't see your hands,' the 'sleeping with that week' — is retroactively explained by this one line. The structure across the cold open is excellent writing, and this line closes the loop. Strong rewatch bonus.

jokes.text: We had a foreign exchange student live with us when I was young and we called him my brother and that's what I thought he was. And then he went home to what is now formerly Yugoslavia, taking all of my blue jeans with him. And I had to spend the entire winter in shorts. That is what Ryan is like. A fake brother who steals your jeans.
jokes.setup: Ryan has told Michael to prepare for major changes. Michael does a talking head to explain his feelings about Ryan.
jokes.punchline: Michael's elaborate Yugoslavia metaphor — culminating in 'a fake brother who steals your jeans' — is a genuinely strange and specific bit of Michael Scott logic.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'formerly Yugoslavia' and the grievance being about blue jeans is what elevates this above a generic Michael ramble. The final summation — 'a fake brother who steals your jeans' — is concise enough to be quotable. The journey from foreign exchange student to political geography to betrayal through denim is classic Michael non-sequitur logic, and it lands.

jokes.text: Good. A lot. Black guys, mostly.
jokes.setup: Ryan asks Kelly how she's doing. She replies she's dating a lot of guys.
jokes.punchline: Kelly specifies 'Black guys, mostly' — not because it's relevant but as a strategic detail designed to provoke Ryan, which is characteristic of Kelly's chaos energy.
jokes.explanation: The specificity is the joke — Kelly volunteers a demographic detail for pure maximum-impact provocation. The pause and 'What?' from whoever responds completes it. Very Kelly: using information as a weapon.

jokes.text: I said no because I was committed to our relationship. / Well, I hope you're still committed, because I'm pregnant. And guess what, buddy? I am keeping it.
jokes.setup: Ryan defends his feelings by saying he turned down Karen Filippelli for Kelly. Kelly escalates.
jokes.punchline: Kelly drops the pregnancy bomb as a power move, then immediately doubles down with 'I am keeping it' before Ryan can even process.
jokes.explanation: Kelly's escalation from 'we need to talk' to 'I'm pregnant' in one exchange is a great character moment — she weaponizes the announcement before Ryan can speak. The 'Do you feel prepared to help me raise a baby?' follow-up is equally good. High impact because the audience knows Kelly well enough to suspect it's probably not true.

jokes.text: We have a date. [Kelly talking head, satisfied]
jokes.setup: Ryan panics about the pregnancy and says they'll talk about it at dinner.
jokes.punchline: Kelly's talking head — triumphant 'We have a date' — reveals the pregnancy was a manipulation tactic to get Ryan to take her to dinner.
jokes.explanation: This is excellent. Two words. The entire scene recontextualizes instantly — Kelly faked a pregnancy to get a dinner date. The satisfaction in her delivery, the perfect economy, and the dark but completely in-character scheming make this one of the episode's best. It's not a punchline you see coming even though in retrospect it's inevitable Kelly. Near-perfect structure.

jokes.text: I've been thinking about things and I wanted to know if you would have dinner with me tonight. / Really? / Yes. / I'll make a reservation. / No, no. Let me cook for you. Cauliflower and noodles. Baked potato on the side. / I would prefer a public place.
jokes.setup: Angela, newly single after breaking up with Dwight over Sprinkles, asks Dwight to dinner — seemingly reconciling.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's enthusiastic 'I'll make a reservation!' is cut off by Angela specifying she wants him to cook — then the menu ('cauliflower and noodles, baked potato on the side') is exactly as joyless as expected from these two. Dwight's 'I would prefer a public place' suggests fear of being alone with Angela after their breakup.
jokes.explanation: The menu — cauliflower and noodles, baked potato — is perfectly joyless for these two characters. Dwight's 'I would prefer a public place' is a good subversion of the expected 'man wants to cook' dynamic. Character-specific throughout.

jokes.text: So, elephant in the room, I have your old job. / Well, not exactly my job. I mean, I had a different title. / Oh, well, excuse me. Same office, same responsibilities. Different salary. You'll get there. Don't worry.
jokes.setup: Jan visits the Scranton branch. Ryan and Jan have an awkward exchange about roles.
jokes.punchline: Ryan's 'you'll get there, don't worry' to Jan — a woman who had the job he now holds, who is significantly older — is delivered with the oblivious condescension of a 26-year-old who doesn't know what he doesn't know.
jokes.explanation: Ryan's condescension toward Jan is a great reversal — she's clearly seething and he's completely tone-deaf. The 'you'll get there' toward someone who already was there and got fired is darkly funny.

jokes.text: What is the actual deal with these things in terms of testicles? / What? / I don't want to grow weird sperm in case we ever want to have kids.
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to figure out his new BlackBerry. Jan is present.
jokes.punchline: Michael's concern about BlackBerry radiation affecting his sperm — asked of Jan without preamble — is both medically unfounded and socially catastrophic as an opener.
jokes.explanation: 'Weird sperm' is a funny phrase. The context — Michael asking this of his girlfriend-boss-ex Jan in a professional setting — amplifies the cringe. Decent but not among the episode's highlights.

jokes.text: He's being a real twerp about it, too. It's all about youth and agility and streamlining and trying to squeeze out the older people. He's such a snake. / I hope he gets hit with an ageism suit.
jokes.setup: Michael complains to Jan about Ryan's presentation. Jan commiserates.
jokes.punchline: Jan — a corporate executive — immediately validates Michael's concerns about ageism and suggests a lawsuit. The irony is she was just condescended to by Ryan herself moments ago.
jokes.explanation: Functional setup for the ageism plot but not especially funny on its own. Jan's pivot to lawsuits is in character but the joke is lightweight.

jokes.text: So older people have just as many rights as younger people? / Yes, Michael. They do.
jokes.setup: Jan explains the Age Discrimination in Employment Act to Michael.
jokes.punchline: Michael's summary question — 'So older people have just as many rights as younger people?' delivered with dawning amazement — reveals he genuinely did not know this.
jokes.explanation: Michael's earnest surprise at a basic civil rights principle is a good beat. Jan's exhausted 'Yes, Michael. They do.' is the perfect straight-man response. Clean and efficient.

jokes.text: Creed? Everything okay? Everything's cool, dude. I'm 30. Well, in November, I'll be 30.
jokes.setup: Michael, worried about age discrimination, checks in on Creed — who is visibly elderly.
jokes.punchline: Creed, who is clearly in his sixties, claims to be 30 — then 'corrects' himself to say he'll be 30 'in November.' He delivers this with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Creed lying about his age so brazenly that he claims to currently be 30, then 'correcting' to an upcoming birthday — as if that's the more accurate detail — is signature Creed Bratton material. It's short, absurdist, and so perfectly in character it couldn't be said by anyone else. The 'dude' to Michael is a nice touch. One of the episode's standout moments.

jokes.text: New ideas are fine, but they are also illegal because they are a form of ageism.
jokes.setup: Michael has called everyone into the conference room to fight Ryan's technology push using the Age Discrimination Act.
jokes.punchline: Michael has extended 'ageism' to cover 'new ideas' themselves — a logical leap so vast it becomes absurdist.
jokes.explanation: Michael has weaponized a real law in an absurd way — 'new ideas are illegal because they discriminate against old ideas.' The confidence of the delivery and the total logical failure is excellent Michael Scott territory. The 'I am right' tag is essential.

jokes.text: Why do we, as a society, hate old people so much? / Because they're lame.
jokes.setup: Michael tries to make a philosophical point about society's treatment of the elderly.
jokes.punchline: Creed — an old person himself — immediately answers 'because they're lame,' undermining Michael's argument from within.
jokes.explanation: The inversion is perfect: Michael's rhetorical question is answered by the person it should most offend, who doesn't register that it applies to him. Creed's total lack of self-awareness is his defining trait, and 'because they're lame' is casual, specific, and devastating. Near-perfect economy.

jokes.text: In fact, many cultures revere old people because of their storytelling ability. Like the old lady from Titanic. Or the funny things that they can do, like 'Where's the Beef?'
jokes.setup: Michael argues against Creed's point by citing cultures that revere the elderly.
jokes.punchline: Michael's examples of respected elderly figures are: (1) a fictional movie character and (2) an 80s fast food commercial slogan. The 'Where's the Beef?' lady as a symbol of elderly wisdom is perfectly wrong.
jokes.explanation: The two examples are perfectly chosen for Michael — a movie character he clearly found moving and a 40-year-old commercial he thinks counts as cultural reverence. The specificity ('Where's the Beef?') makes it funnier than a generic reference would be.

jokes.text: Why do you have the Big Picture up again? You used that already when you burned your foot. / Reusing the Ben Kingsley, too.
jokes.setup: Michael has set up a presentation in the conference room with inspirational visuals.
jokes.punchline: Jim and Dwight note that Michael is reusing visuals from a previous incident (burning his foot on a George Foreman grill), calling him out on recycling motivational content.
jokes.explanation: A solid callback for fans who remember the foot-burn episode. The rewatch bonus is high for long-term viewers. Michael's explanation — he ran out of ink — is a characteristically pathetic reveal.

jokes.text: Who is this old fart? Did you just stagger off the street out of a box or something? Who's this worthless bag of bones?
jokes.setup: Robert Dunder — co-founder of Dunder Mifflin — arrives to Michael's meeting about respecting older people.
jokes.punchline: Michael, in the middle of arguing FOR respect for the elderly, immediately insults the very elderly man who just walked in — before learning who he is.
jokes.explanation: The structural irony is perfect: Michael has been championing elderly rights for the last five minutes, and the instant an elderly person enters, he calls them a 'worthless bag of bones.' 'Did you just stagger off the street out of a box?' is an absurdly specific insult. The comedic structure here — the situational irony catching Michael immediately — is excellent craft.

jokes.text: I'm gonna live for a very long time. My Grandma Schrute lived to be 101. My Grandpa Manheim is 103, and still puttering around down in Argentina. I tried to go visit him once, but my travel visa was protested by the Shoah Foundation.
jokes.setup: The meeting has turned to a general discussion of aging and longevity.
jokes.punchline: Dwight casually mentions his grandfather lives in Argentina, then notes his visa was 'protested by the Shoah Foundation' — implying the grandfather may be a Nazi war criminal. Delivered entirely without self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: This is among the best jokes in the episode and one of the great Dwight jokes in the series. The Shoah Foundation detail is buried in a list of mundane family information (ages, current activities), and Dwight presents it as merely a travel inconvenience — completely missing the implication that his grandfather is a war criminal. 'Still puttering around' for someone possibly 103 and hiding in Argentina is perfect. The dark subversion is earned because it's never stated explicitly, only implied. Exceptional originality and character integration.

jokes.text: And then Mifflin, of course he killed himself later, uh, but I knew Mifflin through the Rotary Club.
jokes.setup: Robert Dunder begins telling the founding story of Dunder Mifflin.
jokes.punchline: 'Of course he killed himself later' — delivered as a parenthetical throwaway, like noting a colleague changed careers — is a startlingly casual reference to suicide.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is entirely in the framing — 'of course he killed himself later' as an 'of course,' as if this is common knowledge or a predictable outcome. It's absurdist dark comedy through understatement. The 'but I knew Mifflin through the Rotary Club' continues the story as if the suicide was the least interesting part. Excellent economy.

jokes.text: And he was at dinner with Beverly and her husband... What was his name? Jerry. Jerry Trupianno... I don't know. From South Jersey and he was tall. / Both he and Mifflin were tall guys.
jokes.setup: Dunder continues his founding story, which the room is politely enduring.
jokes.punchline: Dunder's story has devolved entirely into irrelevant physical descriptions of a supporting character's husband. 'Both he and Mifflin were tall guys' is the only conclusion reached.
jokes.explanation: The comedy of an elderly person losing the thread of a story in real time, with the audience watching them trail off into irrelevant detail, is well-executed. 'Both he and Mifflin were tall guys' as the lone surviving fact is good. The reaction beats from the office during this ramble are part of the joke.

jokes.text: Well, we have learned that you can't teach an old dog new tricks, because it's illegal. And you will go to jail.
jokes.setup: Michael wraps up the Robert Dunder section and summarizes the lesson for Ryan.
jokes.punchline: Michael's takeaway — that the proverb 'can't teach an old dog new tricks' has been confirmed as legally binding — and that violation results in jail time, is another extension of his ageism misunderstanding.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Michael's legal misunderstanding to 'you will go to jail' is a satisfying button on the ageism plot. The certainty with which he delivers 'and you will go to jail' is well-calibrated.

jokes.text: I heard a joke today. / Oh, that's funny. / Yes, it was.
jokes.setup: Dwight and Angela are having their awkward dinner (at home, apparently). The conversation has stalled.
jokes.punchline: Dwight mentions hearing a joke today. Angela says 'Oh, that's funny.' Dwight confirms. Neither tells nor requests the joke. This constitutes their attempt at dinner conversation.
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character comedy. The joke is structural: two people reference a joke without telling it, both agree it was funny, and the topic is dropped. It perfectly captures the emotional austerity of Dwight and Angela as a couple — their version of small talk is an acknowledgment that humor exists somewhere. 'Yes, it was' is a perfect closing beat. This kind of behavioral comedy — the joke IS how they communicate — is the highest form of character writing.

jokes.text: Then don't look in my eyes. Look right here. It's an old sales trick.
jokes.setup: Angela says looking in Dwight's eyes reminds her of her dead cat.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's solution — look somewhere else on his face, citing it as a sales technique — is a completely wrong-register response to an emotional breakup speech.
jokes.explanation: Dwight's emotional intelligence translating a romantic crisis into a sales technique is exactly who he is. 'Look right here' with a gesture to presumably his nose or forehead, combined with 'it's an old sales trick,' is perfectly economical character comedy. The register mismatch — breakup speech met with customer service advice — is the comedy, and it's executed without a wasted word.

jokes.text: Dwight pleads: 'No, please don't do this, monkey.' — his pet name for Angela is 'monkey'
jokes.setup: Angela is breaking up with Dwight.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's desperate plea uses the pet name 'monkey' — which is both unexpectedly tender coming from Dwight and slightly wrong.
jokes.explanation: The pet name 'monkey' for Angela Martin is a perfect absurdist touch — it's the last thing you'd expect Dwight to call someone, and Angela is the last person you'd picture being called 'monkey.' The joke is purely in the collision of character and word.

jokes.text: Ryan wants everything in our company to be about emails and IMs, but I think he is forgetting about the original instant message — letters attached to baskets of food.
jokes.setup: Michael unveils his counter-strategy to Ryan's technology initiative: gift baskets.
jokes.punchline: Michael reframes gift baskets as 'the original instant message' — a genuinely creative but completely wrong equivalence that nonetheless has its own internal logic.
jokes.explanation: This is clever writing. 'The original instant message' applied to food baskets is absurd but follows a kind of Michael logic — immediate communication, but physical. The phrase is quotable and the concept is specific enough to be funny rather than random. One of Michael's better speeches.

jokes.text: I miss you. / Elevators.
jokes.setup: Dwight corners Angela in what appears to be an elevator to express his feelings after their breakup.
jokes.punchline: Angela's response to 'I miss you' is 'Elevators' — she's naming their location to deflect, creating a non-response so flat it works as comedy.
jokes.explanation: One word responding to an emotional appeal. Angela literally describes the elevator they're standing in as her entire response to 'I miss you.' The absolute refusal to engage, delivered as location-naming, is a perfect Angela beat. Maximum economy, completely character-specific.

jokes.text: Fine. / Then I just want to be friends. / Good. / Plus a little extra. Also, I love you.
jokes.setup: Dwight is trying to negotiate the terms of his post-breakup relationship with Angela.
jokes.punchline: Dwight accepts 'just friends,' then immediately adds 'plus a little extra' and 'also, I love you' — each clause walking back the previous agreement within one breath.
jokes.explanation: The structure is excellent — Dwight seemingly accepts the terms, then renegotiates them in real time with escalating emotional disclosures. 'Plus a little extra. Also, I love you.' is a great line because the 'also' treats love as an afterthought, a line item. It's emotionally accurate for Dwight and very funny.

jokes.text: You lied about being pregnant. Right. So? / You really don't understand why that might make me kind of angry? / No. We're never getting back together. / Why not?
jokes.setup: Ryan confronts Kelly about the fake pregnancy. Kelly has no remorse.
jokes.punchline: Kelly's 'So?' in response to 'you lied about being pregnant' — followed by genuine confusion about why Ryan is upset — reveals she sees nothing wrong with using a fake pregnancy as a negotiating tactic.
jokes.explanation: Kelly's 'So?' is perfect — there's no defensiveness, just puzzlement that this is considered a problem. Her 'Why not?' to 'we're never getting back together' is the button, showing she sees no logical connection between fake pregnancies and breakups.

jokes.text: Is the magic gone? / It's funny you bring that up because, yes, it is. / I knew it! / I now find you repulsive. / That's honest.
jokes.setup: Jim asks Pam, now that they're public as a couple, if the magic is gone.
jokes.punchline: Pam immediately confirms the magic is gone and that she finds Jim repulsive. Jim accepts this with mild equanimity. The exchange is clearly a joke, but played straight.
jokes.explanation: The banter is well-calibrated — Pam's 'yes, it is' to 'is the magic gone?' lands because the audience knows it isn't true but it's said with conviction. 'I now find you repulsive' is the escalation and 'that's honest' from Jim is the perfect dry button. A good Jim-Pam moment.

jokes.text: Ever since I was a kid, people have been telling me that I can't do things. 'You can't be on the team.' 'You can't move on to second grade.' Well, now they're telling me I can't win back clients using old-fashioned business methods. We'll see about that. And FYI, I eventually aced second grade, and I was the biggest kid in class.
jokes.setup: Michael gives an inspirational speech to the office about his gift basket mission.
jokes.punchline: Michael's list of adversities — being kept off a team and held back in second grade — followed by the boast that he 'aced' second grade and was 'the biggest kid in class' (because he was the oldest), turns an inspirational moment into a confession of failure.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from sports team to second grade to adult business context as parallel adversities is good. The kicker — 'I was the biggest kid in class' — retroactively reveals the 'ace' was a repeat, not an achievement. The structure of inverting an inspirational speech is well-executed.

jokes.text: Gift baskets are the essence of class and fanciness. They are the ultimate present that a person can receive. / What about cash? With cash you can buy whatever you want, including a gift basket. So it's kind of the best gift ever.
jokes.setup: Michael defends gift baskets as the ultimate gift.
jokes.punchline: Phyllis points out cash is superior to gift baskets, including the ability to purchase a gift basket — logically correct and immediately deflating to Michael's argument.
jokes.explanation: Phyllis's logic is airtight and perfectly deployed against Michael's flowery nonsense. The inclusion of 'including a gift basket' as an example is the sharp edge of the joke. Solid setup/punchline structure.

jokes.text: What about a gift basket full of cash? / Yes. Cash basket. Nice work, Tuna.
jokes.setup: Phyllis has just argued cash beats gift baskets. Jim offers a synthesis.
jokes.punchline: Jim's 'gift basket full of cash' is a joke, but Michael takes it completely seriously and immediately rebrands it 'cash basket' and compliments Jim.
jokes.explanation: 'Cash basket' as Michael's serious rebranding of Jim's throwaway joke is good — Michael adopts it enthusiastically, turning Jim's deadpan into an accidental contribution. The compliment 'nice work, Tuna' is a good button.

jokes.text: I would like to see a website deliver baskets of food to people.
jokes.setup: Michael is driving away on the gift basket mission, confident in his superiority over digital commerce.
jokes.punchline: Michael's challenge — a website can't deliver physical goods — is, of course, exactly what websites (and Amazon) do. He's unaware he's describing e-commerce.
jokes.explanation: There's a sweet dramatic irony here — Michael is describing online retail and doesn't know it. The line has gotten funnier with time (post-Amazon dominance). For the original 2007 audience it was an observational joke about Michael's technological ignorance; now it reads as a perfect historical irony. Good rewatch bonus.

jokes.text: Yes, Kelly is Indian. I understand that's confusing.
jokes.setup: Ryan is on the phone with corporate about outsourcing customer service to India.
jokes.punchline: Ryan has apparently had to explain to corporate that their current customer service rep Kelly is Indian, which has somehow confused their outsourcing math. 'I understand that's confusing' is delivered with barely-contained irritation.
jokes.explanation: The one-sided phone call reveal — corporate is confused that they already have an Indian employee — is a good institutional joke about corporate obtuseness. Ryan's exhausted 'I understand that's confusing' is the right delivery.

jokes.text: Why do you use that thing? / It lets them know where you are at all times. / Who? / The government, spy satellites, private detectives, ex-girlfriends.
jokes.setup: Michael uses a GPS navigation system in the car. Dwight asks why.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's list of who is tracking them via GPS — government, spy satellites, private detectives, ex-girlfriends — delivered as if this is obvious and documented, is a perfect Dwight paranoid worldview.
jokes.explanation: The escalating paranoia list — from 'government' (somewhat plausible) to 'spy satellites' to 'ex-girlfriends' (completely personal) — is exactly Dwight's threat model. The mixture of institutional and personal surveillance in one breath is a nice character touch.

jokes.text: Next night, I'm out at a bar, 2:00 a.m. I figure I'll get a sandwich, 'cause you can get a sandwich any time of the night. I run into Vince Vaughn. / No way. / Literally. / Dude, you are so money, but you don't even know it, but you do.
jokes.setup: Ryan is telling a story about running into Vince Vaughn at a bar.
jokes.punchline: Ryan quotes Vince Vaughn quoting his own movie (Swingers — 'you're so money') back at him, and the 'but you don't even know it, but you do' tag shows Ryan's idol worship while also revealing this exchange may be embellished.
jokes.explanation: Ryan's celebrity name-dropping and the Swingers callback ('you're so money') is decent character work — it fits his new persona. The 'but you don't even know it, but you do' self-contradiction is Ryan at his most insufferable. Functional.

jokes.text: Jim, how awesome is Ryan now? / Yeah. He's definitely something. / What does that mean? / That whole lifestyle, his whole vibe, you find that appealing? / ...He smells like what I think Pierce Brosnan probably smells like.
jokes.setup: Andy effusively praises Ryan's new cool-guy persona and asks Jim to validate it.
jokes.punchline: Andy's enumeration of Ryan's qualities culminates in 'he smells like what I think Pierce Brosnan probably smells like' — a deeply specific speculation about a celebrity's scent as the height of cool.
jokes.explanation: This is a great line. The specificity of Pierce Brosnan (not a generic 'cool guy' but a particular imagined scent), combined with 'what I think' — Andy has not smelled Pierce Brosnan but has formed strong opinions about it — is a perfectly constructed piece of absurdist character comedy. The word 'probably' is essential. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Tuna, check you later. 'Cause he's so money that he doesn't even know it.
jokes.setup: Andy finishes his Ryan appreciation speech to Jim.
jokes.punchline: Andy walks away quoting/misquoting Swingers at Jim as a sign-off, applying the 'so money' compliment to Ryan rather than to Jim (whom he's actually addressing).
jokes.explanation: Andy recycling Ryan's celebrity anecdote as his own conversational exit is a decent character beat but not especially crafted. The running gag function is minor.

jokes.text: How can they not know how much better we are? / I don't know. Sometimes people are just impossible and they make you miserable. That is true. Like Angela in accounting. / Yes. She is nuts.
jokes.setup: Michael and Jim/Phyllis have just been rejected by a client. Michael muses about why people don't recognize quality.
jokes.punchline: Phyllis pivots from discussing difficult clients to complaining about Angela in accounting — the subtext being that Phyllis knows Angela and Dwight have something going on, making her frustration have extra layers.
jokes.explanation: A minor comic beat that connects the episode's various threads but doesn't land as a standalone joke. The Angela dig from Phyllis is mildly funny in context.

jokes.text: Yeah, I'm going to do some mock-ups and then turn those into thumbnails, maybe do some splash frames... I don't know what I'm talking about, but I'm excited.
jokes.setup: Ryan has asked Pam to design the Dunder Mifflin Infinity logo. Pam does a talking head.
jokes.punchline: Pam builds momentum with design jargon, then immediately confesses she doesn't know what she's talking about — but her enthusiasm overrides her ignorance.
jokes.explanation: The self-aware confession after the jargon spiral is a great Pam moment — it fits her trajectory (aspiring artist, receptionist, not quite either) and the genuine excitement landing on top of the confusion is warm and funny. 'I don't know what I'm talking about, but I'm excited' is quotable.

jokes.text: Dwight tells Michael to accept the client is gone: 'He's moving on. We had our chance and we killed it.' — then Michael pivots to pitching the new website
jokes.setup: Michael is refusing to accept that a client won't come back. Dwight tells him it's over.
jokes.punchline: Faced with defeat, Michael accidentally does the one thing that works: pitches Ryan's website — the exact technology he's been fighting against — and the client responds positively.
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural irony: Michael's entire episode-long crusade against technology ends with him accidentally selling the tech product to win back a client. The joke is on Michael's position — the thing he hates is the thing that works. Well-constructed episode-level comedy.

jokes.text: I threw everything I had at that guy and nothing. / That's how it goes sometimes, you know? You lose everything and everything falls apart and eventually you die and no one remembers you.
jokes.setup: Michael is dejected after failing to win back clients. Dwight attempts to console him.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's 'comfort' — you lose everything, it all falls apart, you die, no one remembers you — is the most nihilistic possible reading of a setback, delivered earnestly as consolation.
jokes.explanation: Dwight's version of a pep talk ending in 'eventually you die and no one remembers you' is a wonderful piece of dark character comedy. He genuinely thinks this is helpful. 'That is a very good point, Dwight' from Michael is a perfect straight-man button.

jokes.text: Make a right turn. / Wait, wait. No, no, no. It means bear right. / No. It said right. It said take a right. Up there. / No, no, no, look. It means go up to the right, bear right over the bridge and hook up with 307. / Make a right turn. / Maybe it's a shortcut, Dwight. / It said go to the right. / It can't mean that. / There's a lake there! I think it knows where it is going. / This is the lake! / The machine knows! / This is the lake! / Stop yelling at me!
jokes.setup: Michael is following GPS navigation. Dwight protests that it's directing them into a lake.
jokes.punchline: Michael's 'The machine knows!' as the car drives into a lake is the escalation payoff — Michael's blind faith in technology (which he has been arguing against all episode) gets them driven into a lake.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's set-piece comedy moment and it earns its high scores. The irony is pitch-perfect: Michael has spent the entire episode arguing against technology, but the moment a machine tells him something, he follows it into a lake. 'The machine knows!' is Michael Scott at his most gloriously self-contradictory. The escalating argument — each line ratcheting up panic as the lake approaches — is well-constructed. Structurally, this pays off the anti-technology theme while character-specifically, it shows Michael's authority-deference overriding his own stated beliefs.

jokes.text: Remain calm. I have trained for this. / Exit the window! Here we go.
jokes.setup: The car has just driven into a lake. Michael is panicking.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's crisis response — 'Remain calm. I have trained for this.' — reveals he has specifically prepared for the scenario of being driven into a lake, which is simultaneously reassuring and alarming.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Dwight. Of course he's trained for being driven into a lake. The specificity of the training, implied without elaboration, is funnier than any explanation would be. 'Exit the window! Here we go.' as a drill command in an actual crisis is Dwight in his element. One of the episode's best Dwight moments. High character integration score because no other character on television has this joke available to them.

jokes.text: You sure you're okay? / Fine. / Good. That is what's most important. / Did you get the rental insurance? Because that is pretty important, too, at a time like this.
jokes.setup: Michael and Dwight have survived driving into the lake. Dwight checks on Michael.
jokes.punchline: Dwight pivots immediately from 'that is what's most important' (Michael's safety) to 'did you get the rental insurance?' — demonstrating that Michael's safety and the car insurance are roughly equivalent concerns.
jokes.explanation: The immediate pivot from concern about life to concern about rental paperwork is classic Dwight — practical above emotional. 'Because that is pretty important, too, at a time like this' is the qualifier that makes it exceptional — the 'too' implies equal weight, and 'at a time like this' is a phrase usually reserved for emotional gravitas.

jokes.text: Look at that. Still works. Old-fashioned cell phone.
jokes.setup: Soaking wet after being driven into a lake by GPS, Michael checks his phone.
jokes.punchline: Michael interprets his phone surviving the lake as evidence for his anti-technology thesis — 'old-fashioned' technology beat the new GPS — while standing in a lake having just followed GPS directions into it.
jokes.explanation: Michael's ability to extract his preferred narrative from any evidence — the cell phone surviving proves old technology wins — is a good character moment. He's turned a near-disaster into confirmation of his worldview.

jokes.text: Michael and Dwight march back into the country club, dripping wet, to reclaim the gift basket: 'We're going to reclaim our gift basket. We're going to take what's rightfully ours. Take a stand, Dwight!'
jokes.setup: Michael and Dwight are soaking wet after driving into a lake. The gift basket was left at the last client.
jokes.punchline: Michael treats reclaiming a $30 gift basket as a heroic crusade — marching back through a country club dripping wet to demand its return
jokes.explanation: The visual of two soaking wet men demanding a gift basket back is inherently funny. Michael's grandiose rhetoric ('take what's rightfully ours') applied to a petty commercial situation is his defining comedy mode. The physical element elevates this.

jokes.text: Ryan asks Pam to dinner after approving her logo designs — 'Wear something nice'
jokes.setup: Ryan has been flattering Pam's design work. He asks her to dinner.
jokes.punchline: Ryan adds 'wear something nice' before Pam has even responded — completely presumptuous and revealing that his interest in her designs is at least partly romantic.
jokes.explanation: Ryan's casual sleaziness ('wear something nice' before she's answered) is a good character moment — it shows his new corporate persona has not improved his interpersonal judgment. The cringe is effective.

jokes.text: I guess he can't get any girl he wants.
jokes.setup: Andy has just finished telling Jim that Ryan 'can get any girl he wants.' Cut to Ryan's failed dinner invitation with Pam.
jokes.punchline: Jim's talking head — 'I guess he can't get any girl he wants' — is a dry, satisfied button on Andy's earlier Ryan worship.
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural comedy. Andy spent a minute listing Ryan's attributes, including 'he can get any girl he wants.' The very next scene undercuts this with Ryan failing to ask out Pam. Jim's deadpan callback — barely commenting — is the best possible button. The restraint is everything: Jim doesn't gloat, he just notes it. This is the kind of structural joke that makes The Office writers' room excellent.

jokes.text: Michael and Dwight return dripping wet to the client's office to demand the gift basket back
jokes.setup: Michael declared they would reclaim the gift basket as a matter of principle.
jokes.punchline: Two completely soaking wet men walk into a professional office to demand their gift basket back — the visual absurdity of the situation (inferred from 'my clothes are so wet,' 'my shoes are so muddy') is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The visual gag of two soaked men demanding a gift basket is strong. The dialogue ('Nice leather. Oh, my shoes are so muddy.') suggests they're deliberately dirtying the furniture as leverage — Michael's 'wet friend' framing adds to the absurdity. High impact as a set piece payoff.

jokes.text: What's missing? The turtles. / Where are the turtles? / Where are the turtles? / I ate them, okay? I ate the turtles. They're gone.
jokes.setup: Michael and Dwight have returned, soaking wet, to reclaim their rejected gift basket from the Elmhurst Country Club.
jokes.punchline: The entire basket has been partially eaten. The missing item — chocolate turtles — is what Michael and Dwight focus on, leading a country club employee to confess he ate them.
jokes.explanation: The repeated 'Where are the turtles?' has a good escalating rhythm, and the confession from the employee — delivered presumably after being stared down by two soaking men — is a good payoff. The fact that Michael and Dwight care most about the turtles specifically is character-consistent.

jokes.text: Excuse me, I have an announcement to make. We seem to be missing a box of chocolate turtles with pecans and we will not be leaving the premises until we obtain them. / Hand over the turtles now!
jokes.setup: The country club employee admits eating the turtles.
jokes.punchline: Michael's formal announcement about the missing turtles — treating it as a hostage situation — followed by Dwight's military command 'Hand over the turtles now!' is comic escalation.
jokes.explanation: Two wet men demanding chocolate turtles from a country club is inherently funny. The formal announcement format and Dwight's military 'Hand over the turtles now!' is a good escalation to the absurdity.

jokes.text: We'll bill you.
jokes.setup: The country club employee has admitted eating the turtles and they're gone.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's response to irrecoverable chocolate turtles is 'We'll bill you' — a bureaucratic solution to a $5 confectionery loss, delivered with full business gravitas.
jokes.explanation: Three syllables. The formal, corporate response to eaten chocolates — delivered after all the escalation — is the perfect button. 'We'll bill you' is the most Dwight possible exit from this situation. Maximum economy: the joke is entirely in the register mismatch between the business-speak and the absurdity of the situation.

jokes.text: This office will not be using any new technology ever. / Starting now. / That is not correct.
jokes.setup: Michael returns soaking wet and makes an announcement to the office about technology.
jokes.punchline: Michael announces a blanket ban on new technology, starting now — and Ryan immediately flatly overrides it with 'That is not correct.'
jokes.explanation: Ryan's 'That is not correct' as a four-word power move is good. The gap between Michael's dramatic declaration and Ryan's dismissal is the comedy. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: I drove my car into a lake. / You did what? / I drove my car into a lake. / Why, you may ask, did I do this? / Well, because of a machine. A machine told me to drive into a lake. And I did it.
jokes.setup: Michael explains to the assembled office why he's soaking wet.
jokes.punchline: Michael's deadpan retelling — 'A machine told me to drive into a lake. And I did it.' — is more absurd because he's aware of this and presenting it as evidence against technology rather than his own credulity.
jokes.explanation: The verbal retelling of the lake incident is good — Michael's framing of his own terrible decision as a cautionary tale about technology is self-aware in entirely the wrong way. 'And I did it' as a flat closing beat is well-timed.

jokes.text: Game, set, match. / Point. Scott. Game over. / End of game.
jokes.setup: Michael believes he has proven his anti-technology point with the lake story.
jokes.punchline: Michael delivers three successive sports-conclusion phrases — game, set, match / point Scott / game over — as if the argument has been won at multiple levels simultaneously. Then 'End of game' adds a fourth.
jokes.explanation: The redundant pile-up of sports conclusions is a decent Michael overstatement gag. The 'Point. Scott.' as a separate beat is the funniest part — grammatically it should be 'Point, Scott' but as a two-word declaration it reads differently. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: And computers are about trying to murder you in a lake.
jokes.setup: Michael gives a talking head about the lessons of the day — life, business, human connection.
jokes.punchline: Michael's philosophical summation of the episode — 'and computers are about trying to murder you in a lake' — as the climax of a speech about human connection is a perfect Michael conclusion.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's thematic button and one of its best lines. 'And computers are about trying to murder you in a lake' — presented as a philosophical axiom equivalent to 'life is about human connections' — is perfect. It's quotable, it encapsulates Michael's entire worldview being shaped by a single incident, and it functions as both a great character line and an absurdist punchline to the episode's central conflict. The economy is excellent.

jokes.text: I'm not saying I had a meteoric rise, but I did. And if they knew how much I was paying for my haircut now, they wouldn't be giving me a noogie. It was $200.
jokes.setup: Ryan does a talking head — apparently about people from his past who didn't respect him.
jokes.punchline: 'I'm not saying I had a meteoric rise, but I did' is self-contradictory bluster. The $200 haircut as proof of his success — and the noogie as the indignity he's escaped — is a wonderfully specific portrait of hollow new-money status anxiety.
jokes.explanation: Ryan's closing talking head crystallizes his Season 4 character arc. 'I'm not saying I had a meteoric rise, but I did' is a great self-defeating sentence — the denial and the boast cancel each other out. The $200 haircut as the mark of success, and the noogie as the injury to be revenged, is perfectly observed status anxiety. A strong final character note.

tmdb_overview: Ryan returns to Scranton with a plan to bring Dunder Mifflin into the digital age by launching a new website - Dunder Mifflin Infinity. Michael is worried about ageism and attempts to win back clients using old fashion business skills. Relationships are on the forefront as Ryan returns to an eager Kelly, Jim and Pam are outed to the office, and Angela is still upset with Dwight about her cat.
